problem: Prior VLM/LLM-based goal navigation matches language to raw images, which only tells where an image was taken, not the coordinates of a target object, so it cannot support locating and fetching. Semantic SLAM is limited to closed-set categories.
motivation: A fetch-and-place robot must know object coordinates, and objects in the real world are too diverse for closed-set categories. The authors propose storing open-vocabulary object-level features together with their 3D locations, so that natural-language queries can be resolved to coordinates without re-exploring.
key_idea: Build an object-level Visual Scene Representation by segmenting objects with SAM, encoding each with the CLIP visual encoder and attaching a map-frame 3D position, built via an active TSP-based coverage path, then query it with CLIP text features while GPT-4 decomposes instructions into API calls.
insight: Object-level crops with coordinates work better than whole-image matching (LM-Nav, used as the raw-image ablation) because small objects are diluted in full images and image matching yields no object position. SAM segments plus CLIP also beat closed-set-trained LSeg and detector-based open-vocabulary methods (ViLD, OWL-ViT v2), which produce more false positives and struggle with stacked-object locations. Evidence is limited to one small real-lab query test.
method: Object feature extraction: SAM segments almost all objects in the RGB image, holes are filled with original pixels, and each crop is encoded by the CLIP visual encoder into a 512-d feature.
Object localization: the center pixel of each instance is back-projected to a map-frame 3D point using depth, camera intrinsics and robot localization; the tuple (feature, position) is stored.

Active coverage: the 2D SLAM map is binarized, opened morphologically, boundaries are extracted with the Suzuki algorithm and simplified by polygon fitting, and the points are ordered clockwise so the side-facing camera views the objects.

Graph and TSP: polygon vertices form a graph with Euclidean edge costs, other edges are set to a large cost, and a TSP/Hamiltonian path including the start position is solved to get the coverage route.
VSR query: the text is encoded by the CLIP text encoder, the dot product with all stored features is computed, and the argmax object's coordinates are returned, zero-shot.
LLM task planning: GPT-4 with chain-of-thought few-shot prompts decomposes instructions into atomic APIs (search, navigate, pick, place, done).

setting.backbone: SAM + CLIP (frozen) for the scene representation; GPT-4 (frozen) for planning
setting.observation: RGB-D cameras (head and arm-tip, 640x480) + 2D lidar + SLAM map and localization
setting.action_space: high-level API calls (navigate to coordinate, pick, place) on a mobile manipulator
setting.privileged: 2D SLAM map of the environment is used for the coverage planning; no other privileged information

numbers.eval_set_note: 20 object queries and 10 location queries in a real laboratory
numbers.extra: real robot lab; queries evaluated on images captured during active coverage; the text says 85% object and 80% location while the table counts 17/20 objects and 8/10 locations

numbers_note: Only a small real-world query-matching table; no standard navigation benchmark. The text says 85% object and 80% location, and Table I lists 83 overall (which does not match 25/30). The instruction-following experiments are qualitative only.
results: On 30 real-lab queries, VSR reaches 83% success versus OWL-ViT v2 70%, ViLD 57%, LM-Nav 47% and LSeg 23%. The full system follows instructions such as 'put away the black coke can' through GPT-4 plans, shown qualitatively.
limitations: Tiny, non-standard, single-lab evaluation with no standard benchmarks or quantitative end-to-end task success
Static scene assumption: the map is pre-built and objects may move afterwards; dynamic scenes are left as future work
Requires a pre-built 2D map and a full coverage pass before use
